name: Tara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at Saltvale, a potash mine. Potash is a salt they use for fertiliser. The continuous miner is a machine with a big spinning drum at the front that chews through the salt wall, and I steer it with a remote box on a strap while walking beside it. It's a kilometre down, dry and warm, and everything's pinkish white. I like that you can see your progress at the end of a shift. What I don't like is the noise, and that my husband Ole and I are on opposite rosters half the time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He's an electrician there, keeps the conveyors and the miners running. So both our pay packets come from the same hole in the ground. We've got good savings and a little cabin by the lake that we rent out in summer, but I think about that one-mine thing more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, back to work. I'd probably mention it at dinner with the neighbours. I'm not someone who posts about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. The one-mine thing scares me more than AI does, so if AI fizzles, I've just got the old worry about potash prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep saving, keep renting the cabin, keep using the AI tools for the cabin bookings, because it's quicker for answering guests. That's all I use it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, but I'd still have Saltvale on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the old worry about potash prices. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fertiliser prices go up and down, and when they're low the mine cuts shifts. We had a bad year when Nils was a baby, and Ole lost overtime and I lost a crew. That's the kind of thing I actually lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI tools for with the cabin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing replies to guests, mostly, and sometimes the listing. Freya showed me how. It saves me twenty minutes a night, and I'd never have tried it if she hadn't sat me down.

S0.say: I'd say good, back to work, and mention it at dinner with the neighbours. I don't post about things online.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because having both our jobs at one mine scares me more than AI does. If AI fizzles, I'm left with the old worry about potash prices.
S0.do: Keeps saving and keeps renting out the lake cabin. Keeps using AI tools to reply to cabin guests because it saves time each night.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with Saltvale's ups and downs still in mind.
S0.quote: The one-mine thing scares me more than AI does, so if AI fizzles, I've just got the old worry about potash prices.
S0.fieldNote: Tara's real worry is concentration risk: two incomes from one mine. AI barely registers in this picture beyond the cabin replies her daughter taught her. The memory of a bad price year when her son was a baby sets her baseline for what trouble looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a few hard years, so the mine and the union should sit down and plan it properly. I'd say that at work. Nothing loud, just practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think continuous miners are already going remote at some potash mines, so this speeds it up. Ole's job is probably safer than mine, because someone has to fix the things. So the one-mine worry gets worse, but in a lopsided way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company about the remote operator training in the first few months, but only once I'd seen how it worked for the first group. We'd put more into savings and maybe hold off on the new roof for the cabin. And Ole and I would have the talk about one of us working somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd want a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be the one to leave Saltvale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ole, because electricians can work anywhere, there are three mines and a power station within an hour. It'd be a pay cut for him, but we'd sleep better. He'd grumble, he likes his crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see the first group before taking the remote training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen courses that lead nowhere. If the first group gets jobs in the control room, I'll sign up the next week. If they get shown the door, I'll know.

S1.say: I'd say it's going to be a few hard years, so the mine and the union should sit down and plan it properly. I'd say that at work, practical rather than loud.
S1.think: I think continuous miners are already going remote at some potash mines, so this speeds it up. Ole's repair job is safer than mine, so the one-mine worry gets worse in a lopsided way.
S1.do: Plans to take the remote operator training once she sees how the first group fares. Saves more, delays the cabin's new roof, and discusses her husband moving to another employer to spread the risk.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, and wanting a plan.
S1.quote: If they get shown the door, I'll know.
S1.fieldNote: Tara's steadiness shows in her wait-and-check approach to retraining: she'll go second, not first. Her main move is spreading the household's risk across two employers. Being in the middle politically, she wants planning rather than protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast and the government has to step in with something, at least for the mining towns. At work I'd be in every meeting. I'd probably post for once, because people would need to see they're not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think both of us go. If AI can do almost any job, it can fix a conveyor too, maybe a year after it can drive a continuous miner. So the thing I've been afraid of, both of us at once, happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away: no holidays, no new car, nothing that isn't the mortgage and the kids. Ole would start looking at jobs off the mine right away, because even a year's head start matters. We'd sell the cabin if we had to, and I'd talk to my sister about whether we could stay with her for a while if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the nightmare I've had for ten years, just with robots in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Freya and Nils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya's fifteen and would figure it out herself, so I'd tell her straight. Nils is eleven, I'd tell him Mum and Dad are changing jobs, which might even be true. I'd try not to cry in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough to clear a good chunk of the mortgage, maybe all of it if we sell the cabin. It isn't enough to learn anything new. So it's money time, not learning time.

S2.say: I'd say this is far too fast and the government has to step in, at least for mining towns. I'd be in every meeting at work and might post so people know they're not alone.
S2.think: I think both of us go: if AI can drive a continuous miner, it can fix a conveyor a year later. The thing I've feared, both of us at once, happens.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage and the children, and her husband starts looking for work off the mine immediately. Considers selling the lake cabin and asks her sister about staying with her if things get bad.
S2.feel: Alarmed; it's the nightmare she has had for ten years, now with robots in it.
S2.quote: That's the nightmare I've had for ten years, just with robots in it.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI lands squarely on Tara's long-standing fear of both incomes failing together. She thinks in money terms, not learning terms, about the two years. Asking her sister for a place to stay shows how far she'd go even with solid savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough time if everyone gets moving. I'd want the company and the government to put up retraining money, and I'd say that at work and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to split us up, job-wise. Ole goes to the power station in year one, I take the remote training in year two, and we're not both in the same basket when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ole would move jobs early. I'd do the remote operator course once the first group has gone through. We'd clear the mortgage by year four if we can, and keep the cabin as a backup. Freya's university plans might change, she wanted to do engineering, and I'd want her to look at things with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. It's a race, but we'd be running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years feel different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between a plan and a scramble. With two years we're cutting and selling. With five years we're moving pieces around on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Freya's plans. Would she agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, she'd tell me engineers will build the robots. She might be right. I'd just want her to have a second string to her bow, like I wish I'd had.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but enough if everyone gets moving. I'd want the company and government to fund retraining, and I'd say so at work and at the union.
S3.think: Five years is enough to split our jobs apart: Ole to the power station, me into remote training. Then we're not both in the same basket when it hits.
S3.do: Her husband moves jobs early, and she takes remote operator training once the first group finishes. Aims to clear the mortgage by year four and keep the cabin as a backup, and rethinks her daughter's study plans.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like running a race rather than watching one.
S3.quote: With five years we're moving pieces around on purpose.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Tara do exactly the thing she's wanted for years: spread the family's risk across two employers. Her plan is orderly and sequenced. She's thoughtful about her daughter's choices but open to being wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. I'd want the company to start planning now. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for us. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage paid, the kids through school. I could work at Saltvale until near the end and then do something with the cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ole would move to the power station in a few years, not right away. I'd keep working, take the remote training when it comes, and we'd think about building a second cabin by the lake to rent out. Freya and Nils would plan their studies with this in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more in the background. Like knowing winter's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second cabin? Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will still want a holiday by a lake, I think. It's something we own, not something a company can take away. I'd want to see it working for a couple of summers before we borrowed for it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger colleague in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a second skill and not to have both incomes in one place. That's my whole lesson from twenty years. They'd probably ignore me, like I would have.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody has an excuse to be caught out. I'd tell people at work the company should start planning now.
S4.think: Ten years is good for us: at 53 the mortgage is paid and the kids are through school. I could work at Saltvale until near the end and then do something with the cabin.
S4.do: Keeps working and takes remote training when offered, while her husband moves to the power station in a few years. Considers building a second rental cabin, and the children plan their studies with the change in mind.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, like knowing winter is coming.
S4.quote: It's something we own, not something a company can take away.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Tara's caution into a gradual plan built around owning something. She is careful even about the second cabin and wants to see results first. Her one lesson for younger workers is to spread their risk, which runs through every scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of us would go at once with no time to split up. What would help is real notice, something like a year's warning from the company before any job goes, and income support for families where both people worked at the same place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Lots of people at Saltvale are married to someone else at Saltvale. Nobody plans for that, and it doubles everything.

headlineQuote: Lots of people at Saltvale are married to someone else at Saltvale.
portrait: Tara Jensen is 43 and runs a continuous miner a kilometre underground at the Saltvale potash mine, where her husband Ole is an electrician. Her deepest worry, long before AI, is that both their pay packets come from one mine. Strong savings and a rental cabin by the lake keep her calm in the gentle pictures, but fast AGI hits her exact nightmare of both jobs going at once. With five or ten years she calmly sequences a plan: Ole moves employers, she retrains once others have proved the course, and the family builds on what it owns.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because both she and her husband would lose their jobs at once with no time to spread the risk.
whatWouldHelp: A year's notice from the company before any job goes, and income support for families where both partners worked at the same mine.
